newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Troop movements as Zaire waits for government.
newsitem.headline: Troop movements as Zaire waits for government.

text.p: KINSHASA, Dec 23 (reuter) - Troops manned potential points of unrest in the Zaire capital on Monday in advance of the expected naming by President Mobutu Sese Seko of a prime minister to deal with rebel fighting, residents said.
The heavier than normal troop presence was noticeable around the main university campus outside Kinshasa and on access routes into the capital.
There was no official comment on a French news report that the Zairean army had started a counter-attack against Tutsi-led rebels who have seized a swathe of border land in eastern Zaire.
French Television 2 teletext service, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, quoted rebel leader Laurent Kabila as saying the attack began in Bunia, near the Ugandan border, on Saturday.
"There are regular troop reinforcements in Bunia and attacks (taking place)", Kabila was quoted as saying. He said his troops were resisting.
He called on Kinshasa authorities to "halt the military venture and come to the negotiating table", and accused France of helping Mobutu in his plan to push back the rebels.
Mobutu returned last Tuesday after more than four months of cancer treatment and rest in Europe. He has vowed to resist Rwandan-backed ethnic Tutsi rebels who took up arms in October.
A deadline set by Mobutu for political leaders to agree among themselves on the crisis government expired at midday Monday, leaving the responsibility with president.
Allies of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo said on state radio on Monday any move to oust the incumbent would be unconstitutional.
"Article 79 of the constitution gives the dispositions for the departure of the prime minister," Delphin Kapaya, an opposition politician backing Kengo, said on state radio.
"For today, since the prime minister has not died, resigned or been removed by parliament, and in the absence of a coup d'etat, there is no vacancy at his office," he added.
Supporters of radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi have warned of trouble unless he is reappointed prime minister. He was sacked in 1993 after briefly holding the job.

In normal circumstances Mobutu is not empowered to nominate the prime minister and his cabinet. But his spokesman, Kabuya Lumuna, said at the weekend the president could use emergency clauses of the constitution.
He said one possibility was for the president to use emergency wartime powers to appoint the government.

"Constitutionally the only thing the president could have done to change the prime minister was to instruct his men in parliament to vote him out. But the procedure could have taken weeks and we are at a time of crisis," a senior legal source told Reuters.
